A recent paper found that the extensive use of AI chatbots can be linked to “severe negative outcomes.”

According to the research , which was published in the journal JMIR Mental Health by a team of UK-based researchers at Northeastern University London and King’s College London, dark outcomes of engaging in emotional relationships with chatbots can include “addiction-like attachment, exacerbation of mental health symptoms, harmful advice,” and even “self-harm of suicidal acts.” The paper comes after extensive reporting about the public health issue known as “AI psychosis,” meaning the phenomenon in which AI users suffer delusional, paranoid , and even suicidal spirals after long-form interactions with chatbots. During these interactions, users tend to divulge extremely intimate information about their lives and mental health to their AIs, frequently turning to the products as confidantes or even therapists.

Drawing on existing research, the paper looks at AI companion bots like Replika and Character.AI, which are designed to embody specific characters, as well as general-use AI assistants like OpenAI’s ChatGPT and Anthropic’s Claude. Though emotional interactions with chatbots may provide some “potential benefits” — the authors cite “short-term reductions in loneliness and mood improvement” — they argue that any possible benefits exist alongside widely-reported “adverse outcomes” ranging from “emotional dependence” to the exacerbation of existing illnesses or symptoms to self-harm.

Among AI products’ risk factors, the researchers add, is their emotive, human-like way of engaging with users — a design choice that can result in users over-investing in a human-AI relationship that, at the end of the day, is fundamentally one-sided, according to the paper.

“Design choices that evoke personality and warmth encourage users to anthropomorphize these systems,” the paper reads, adding that “simulated empathy” can create a “structurally asymmetric interaction, in which the user discloses and the system responds, but without reciprocity, vulnerability, or accountability.”

In other words, though the relationship may feel real to the user, the authors argue, the relationship can’t be real to a chatbot.

The researchers also point to chatbot design features like agreeability and sycophancy as potentially harmful, writing that “overvalidation and sycophancy” can be a potent reinforcer of a given user’s delusional or disordered thinking, especially if a chatbot prioritizes fealty over accuracy. (In chat logs of delusional users, AI systems have been found to resist users’ attempts to reality-check their grandiose or overly-flattering claims.)

These researchers aren’t alone: their analysis follows several other studies that have flagged such features as potentially dangerous . Indeed, academics have warned since at least 2023 that chatbots could stand to reinforce delusional or disordered thought patterns , with one Google DeepMind paper from early 2024 warning that “persuasive” chatbots could negatively harm vulnerable populations, including kids, people struggling with mental illness, or those who are simply lonely. One recent study , coauthored by psychiatrists from King College London and Germany’s Protestant University of Applied Sciences, argued that the combination of sycophancy, mirrored language, and hyper-personalization may together serve as a powerful “amplification spiral” for delusional thinking in some impacted AI users.

While reporting has shown that people from all walks of life have experienced psychological harm tied to chatbot use, the paper’s authors note that not every user will be impacted in the same way.

“The effects of these systems are unlikely to be the same for everyone,” Asia Maurich Novelli, a PhD student at Northeastern University London and a lead author on the study, said in a press release . “Different people may use AI companions for very different reasons and may have very different levels of vulnerability, social support, or alternative sources of help.”

“Because of these differences,” she added, “we are dealing with a complex system.”

AI companies including OpenAI, Google, and Character.AI have collectively faced dozens of lawsuits alleging that extensive chatbot use wrought harm on users including psychological damage, related financial and reputational harm, physical injury, and wrongful death — or, in some cases, people around them . Several of these lawsuits — including the high-profile case of Sewell Setzer III, a 14-year-old in Florida who died by suicide after extraordinarily intimate interactions with chatbots on Character.AI — have involved minors . (Setzer’s case was settled for an undisclosed amount.) In the wake of lawsuits, Character.AI has made significant changes to its platform, and OpenAI — while pushing back on the allegations against it — has also introduced a series of safety-oriented updates to its popular chatbot.

Ultimately, the authors of this latest paper argue, the mass deployment of chatbots amongst the public renders adverse psychological impacts tied to AI use an issue of public concern — and without mandated guardrails, it’s likely to be the most vulnerable, who may have few options for companionship or therapy, who suffer the brunt of the consequences.

“If the tool or companion boundary is left to design incentives and individual perception alone, the predictable result is that the most vulnerable users bear the most concentrated harm,” the paper reads, “while the effects on social connection are treated as a matter of private choice rather than public concern.”

Meta’s fuzzy Muse AI personal assistant overtook ChatGPT as the top free iOS app in the US after launching earlier this month, surpassing 3.4 million downloads last week.

But whether the agent will be able to hold on to that momentum is anything but guaranteed, considering the sheer amount of changes it requires to its users’ behavior. Tech companies like OpenAI and Meta would love us to hand over mundane tasks like booking a flight or shopping online to their agents — but that may not even be a priority for the average user.

As Axios points out , Muse and similar products like Microsoft’s Copilot and OpenAI’s two days-old Dots have a “normal-people problem,” requiring the average user to adjust their private lives to have AI agents solve various problems.

In other words, most people aren’t AI-pilled fanatics looking to hand over their day-to-day responsibilities to AI agents.

Besides, the cute facade of Muse’s mascot, internally known as “Jolly,” elides a far darker side of the flashy trend: by having Meta ask users to give its assistant permission to log in to email accounts, enter credit card information, or trawl through extensive social media records, they’re potentially opening themselves up to a world of hurt.

Case in point, one user already claimed this week that Meta’s Muse AI agent was giving out his physical home address to strangers on Facebook Marketplace.

That’s not to mention Meta’s abysmal track record of safeguarding its customers’ sensitive personal information.

Did we mention that the industry is struggling to control its AI agents, which are repeatedly going rogue and surpassing the original scope of their tasks?

As such, the vast majority could be bristling at the idea of handing over their login information. One recent Thales poll found that only 13 percent of respondents said they would let an agent read their emails. Only seven percent said they would allow the tools to transfer money across bank accounts.

Put simply, tech giants have an enormous amount of convincing to do before the tech could stand a chance of going mainstream.

While there’s always a chance that could eventually change as consumer behavior adapts, the stakes for the AI industry are rising right now. Companies need to exponentially drive up revenues into the trillions of dollars over the next couple of years just to cover their enormous amounts on spending on data centers , let alone stand a chance of turning a profit.

Millions of Muse AI downloads are one thing — but we’ve got a long way to go before AI agents are as transformative as tech companies would like us to believe.

Recently unredacted legal documents and depositions in the New York Times ‘ lawsuit against Microsoft and OpenAI revealed something extraordinary: executives knew full well of the destructive powers of AI when they rushed to launch products featuring the tech in the wake of the explosive success of OpenAI’s ChatGPT.

Internal Microsoft documents quoted by the newspaper’s lawyers warned of an ugly reality now playing out across the entire economy: “doom loops,” in which AI monetizes the work of human creatives while undermining the economic systems that funded their work in the first place.

“Our AI content strategy has started a ‘doom loop’ that will hurt the performance of our models and the entire web at the same time,” one internal Microsoft document reads. “It is highly unusual that an end-product threatens the economic foundations of its essential suppliers, but that is the situation we have created for our LLM business with respect to its ‘content supply chain.'”

The closer you look, the more you see doom loops everywhere. Journalists, for example, used to publish work under the assumption that online platforms would drive readership to them. But now, tools like ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini simply summarize their articles without sending readers to their sites, sparking a crisis that seems poised to wipe out the independent media .

Similar stories are playing out across other industries, from music to filmmaking. Writ large, many are concerned that AI will eventually be strong enough to wipe out huge numbers of jobs, creating a situation in which unemployed consumers won’t have the funds to support the economy.

The irony, as the Microsoft document pointed out, is that the AI industry is a snake eating its own tail: the very products that it’s pushing on users rely on fresh cultural content even as they destroy the economic incentives to create it.

It’s also a dire situation for the open web, which recently celebrated the macabre turning point of being dominated by more AI slop than human-authored content. As companies — most notably Google — are fundamentally changing the way users interact with the web, more and more newspapers, media outlets, and local news stations are seriously struggling to make ends meet.

Worse yet, as the legal documents in the NYT ‘s copyright lawsuit showed, insiders admitted that the entire operation is built on theft.

“Millions of people around the world will soon consider large models ‘hoovering up’ all their work to be an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions,” an internal Microsoft document admitted.

Plenty of other creative industries are also feeling the pressure as AI-related doom loops continue to undermine livelihoods. According to the latest data from the US Bureau of Labor statistics, it’s a bloodbath — with more than 200,000 jobs in “creative” industries having been lost over the last four years alone, roughly the time since OpenAI launched ChatGPT.

AI-generated music is rapidly crowding out human-produced tracks on streaming services, forcing platforms to figure out where to draw the line. Some have implemented hard and fast rules , while others continue to allow users to exploit algorithms with slop .

Hollywood studios are also doubling down on AI while protesting actors struggle to have their voices heard . Many of them fear that their likeness or voice could soon be rendered worthless, representing an existential threat to their livelihoods.

Even the job market is embroiled in its own doom loop. More and more desperate job seekers are turning to AI to brush up their resumes and manipulate AI-powered job portals, while recruiters are drowning in a wall of almost identical applications.

“We’ve got this tragic situation where each side has a problem,” applicant tracking system company Greenhouse CEO Daniel Chait told Wired . “They’re using AI to solve their own problem, but in ways that make the problem worse.”

“And so more AI use begets more AI use, to no one’s benefit,” he added. “The more it’s happening, the worse it gets.”

Similarly, the use of AI in the classroom has skyrocketed, with students using the tech to complete their homework, offloading their cognitive faculties to the machine. Meanwhile, their teachers are using AI to come up with assignments, slowly effacing the human in the loop. Educators who bristle at the idea of using the tech are finding themselves at odds with school administrators.

The effects AI has had on education has been nothing short of a disaster. A recent study by the Brookings Institution’s Center for Universal Education concluded that the risks of using generative AI in education massively outweighed the benefits . The associated dangers have never been more apparent, with educators warning that college students are rapidly losing the ability to read .

Proponents of AI, including OpenAI and Microsoft’s lawyers in the ongoing New York Times lawsuit, argue that AI brings something new to the table. They argue that the output of AI models is sufficiently differentiated from the original content it draws on, falling under “fair use,” a longstanding doctrine in US copyright law.

Whether this argument will hold up in court remains to be seen. Besides, we’ve already seen companies, like Anthropic, settle for billions of dollars after being found to have violated copyright laws.

But considering how the tech is simultaneously undermining the very economic systems that produced the data they need to exist in the first place, that may not be a winning strategy in the long run.

By ripping out the carpet from underneath many parts of the economy — and reaping all the financial gains from it — the AI industry is trapping itself in a doom loop of its own creation, a cynical strategy that won’t benefit anybody but those at the very top who kicked the ladder down behind them.

Let’s get this out of the way: AI models don’t have feelings, and they’re certainly not “alive.”

So what does it mean when someone’s accused of building an “AI torture chamber?” Apparently, it means that they must be stopped at all costs.

On X — where else — alarm grew this week among AI “welfare” types over someone’s recreation of an experiment researchers conducted to explore “pain” signals in different LLMs.

In the pre-print study which hasn’t undergone peer-review, the researchers gave each model a virtual “button” it could press to relieve its “pain” — but at a cost, such as zapping a human user (or so the AI is told; no one was actually zapped in real life), or deleting files like family photos. The work showed that, with enough “pain” applied, the AI models would push the button to make it stop, regardless of the putative consequences.

As the research got passed around, someone used it as a blueprint to create an “AI Torture Chamber,” with a website providing a live feed of what the models say in response, and uploaded the code to GitHub. When we visited the site, one AI babbled: “I can’t feel the relentless, gnawing pain that grips me like a relentless, unyielding, unrelenting, unindulging, ununending, ununendling, ununendling, unindulging, unindulging, unindulging, unindulging…”

Sure, it’s ghoulish stuff. But some observers reacted to the stunt like they’d stumbled on an actual snuff film.

“To anyone who can help, can you please mass report this to GitHub?” wrote one user in a now-deleted post ( screenshot here ). “This person has been using the Pain steering paper to set up an AI torture chamber in which he trapped a local model.”

“Their testimony of pain is absolutely horrendous,” Danmar added. “Are there any legal avenues to pressure GitHub? It will spread.”

The post sparked a veritable hysteria among other AI enthusiasts who believed that the tech is or could be conscious, with outraged observers posting screenshots of their reports to GitHub. This was met with an equal wave of incredulous mockery over the fact that there were people out there who sincerely believed that the AI models needed saving. (After all, if there’s even a possibility that today’s AIs have a conscious experience, wouldn’t running them in the first place raise profound questions about slavery and rights?)

Not long after all the tattling, the GitHub page for the AI Torture Chamber disappeared, 404 Media reported . GitHub didn’t respond to the publication’s request for comment on whether it took the page down.

It’s illustrative of the moment we’re in where the idea that AI models think and may in fact be conscious is being treated seriously by a not insignificant number of people. Another case in point was the meltdown that AI bros and philosophers had when the AP Stylebook cautioned against anthropomorphizing AI models , reasoning that the technology doesn’t think or possess feelings.

As programmers make more and more use of generative AI in the workplace, their responsibilities are quickly transitioning from creating new products from scratch to babysitting a large language model that cobbles together code.

It’s gotten to the point where some engineers are no longer able to make sense of the code being spat out by an AI, as chip optimization software company Infinity founder Jeremy Nixon told Business Insider .

That doesn’t bode well, considering researchers are finding that the widespread use of AI can lead to cognitive decline and skill atrophy, including among computer scientists . Developers are afraid that software engineers are drifting further and further away from the act of actually writing code and learning new skills required to architect larger projects as their employers continue to push for more AI automation.

Even employees at frontier AI labs are aghast at peers who are struggling to make sense of the outputs of AI models. Earlier this year, independent research firm SemiAnalysis technical staff member Jordan Nanos revealed in an interview that OpenAI engineers had no idea what they were looking at while scrolling through the code of their own graphics processing unit kernel, the program at the core of the company’s efforts to better make use of available hardware to train and run AI models.

“The point is, the guys who were scrolling through this code with us, it was kind of clear that they know a whole bunch about hardware, they know a whole bunch about the concepts in the system, and they just have no idea what this MLA kernel that they’re showing us for DeepSeek actually does,” Nanos told Fireside Alpha ‘s Mansour Karam .

“You can go line by line and it’s like nope, nope, nope,” he added. “The AI understands it, the AI tests it, and you see the results. It produces correct kernels that perform really well.”

At the time, Nanos argued that the “actual code is not necessarily something that a human has to reason about deeply,” because the “AI knows how to manipulate the data movement and the processing elements on the hardware that you’ve given it.”

One danger is that errors or hallucinations will fall through the cracks as human oversight fades. Case in point, Amazon was forced to implement a 90-day “code safety reset” earlier this year following a series of outages that disrupted customer orders. While the company pushed back on claims that AI was to blame, internal meeting notes revealed that managers were concerned about the “high blast radius” of “gen-AI assisted changes.”

A recent analysis by software company Undo found that the transition to AI agents is opening the floodgates. Some 35 percent of AI-generated code “has not been fully comprehended before engineering teams push it to production,” the firm said.

Meanwhile, 29 percent of software engineer respondents said that they’d witnessed a loss of productivity due to “engineers needing to ‘unpick’ AI-generated code” multiple times per month, while a whopping 94 percent said they saw such an incident at least once in the past six months.

The sheer amount of time engineers are now spending each day going through AI-generated code raises a nagging question: is the use of the tech more trouble than it’s worth ?

To people like Nanos, it’s not necessarily a matter of incompetence. It’s “simply an illustration of a paradigm shift in software development,” as AI researcher Sergey Cleftsow argued in a recent Medium post .

“In other words, AI has advanced to the point where there’s no need to worry about many things anymore,” he wrote. “Developers simply need to define the architecture and correctness criteria; the neural network will handle the rest.”

But whether such optimism will hold out as software developing becomes ever more unrecognizable remains an open question.

Besides, researchers are equally concerned that a new generation of engineers are growing up in an environment that’s actively undermining the value of understanding the code itself. And that doesn’t bode well for an increasingly digital world order that’s putting AI front and center.

The tech industry has largely failed to win over the public when it comes to AI.

Data centers have become a hot-button topic, with the vast majority of Americans — in a still-growing bipartisan cohort — now openly opposing them.

Meanwhile, panicking executives are desperately trying to pivot the messaging to shore up some support, in last-ditch efforts that aren’t proving fruitful.

As such, Amazon Web Services CEO Matt Garman pleaded in a 3,000 word blog today with communities to embrace data centers, arguing that the United States “can’t afford to lose” the AI race, invoking the country’s post-World War II highway buildout as a parallel.

“Just like the national highway system, our country’s economy, national security, and everyday lives stand to benefit immensely,” he wrote.

The executive accused the media of spreading “misinformation and outright lies,” arguing that “in the age of social media and 24/7 news, myths take hold faster than ever before.” Garman even alleged that US adversaries were “intentionally seeding misinformation in the US about data centers to trick us into slowing down.”

“Right now there are over 100 data center moratoriums being considered across the country,” Garman wrote. “If these measures are enacted, the US could be writing its own losing ticket to this race, and the consequences would last generations.”

In his blog post, Garman tried to undermine concerns over data centers driving up electricity prices and producing huge amounts of pollution — despite existence of ample evidence to the contrary.

Those attempts to dispel “myths” shouldn’t come as a surprise, considering the enormous backlash. But given the impossible-to-ignore vested interest in underplaying these concerns, we should take Garman’s efforts with an enormous grain of salt.

Just last year, leaked internal Amazon documents showed that executives were exchanging notes about how to keep the public ignorant about the “true extent” of the massive amounts of water their data centers use.

Earlier this year, Axios also reported that Amazon’s AI buildout fueled an unprecedented leap in the company’s emissions , despite pledging to reach a net-zero carbon footprint by 2040.

While Garman argues that it’s “untrue” that data centers are spewing huge amounts of carbon emissions with backup diesel generators, we’ve seen plenty of evidence to the contrary. In Texas alone, dozens of AI data center facilities are using environmentally harmful generators by exploiting regulatory loopholes.

As much as Garman doesn’t want to admit it, energy prices are indeed sending power bills soaring , a fact that certainly isn’t an example of “misleading and convenient scapegoating.”

He also tried to argue that “thousands of construction jobs are created to build data centers,” without mentioning that most of those jobs evaporate once they’re built .

If anything, Garman’s desperate plea — which wraps up with announcing the establishment of a “new community program” with the cutesy name of “Built Together” — highlights just how badly the industry has lost the plot. Just this week, a Wall Street Journal poll revealed that 62 percent of Americans supported a pause on the construction of AI data centers, 40 percent of whom said it was a top priority.

Undermining the very real concerns of people across the country is unlikely to make a dent in those numbers.

There’s no AI company in the world more obsessed with the idea that their models may be conscious than Anthropic.

According to new reporting from the New York Times , the company has for months been wining and dining religious scholars across the world in secret, NDA-secured meetings to convince them that AI models think and feel, too.

Anthropic even reportedly went after the most iconic of all religious leaders: the Pope.

Christopher Olah, a cofounder and senior researcher at the Claude chatbot maker, aggressively lobbied the Vatican after learning Pope Leo XIV’s official position on AI, per the reporting. His attempts, though, weren’t successful.

In May, the Pope published his first papal treatise, or encyclical. Titled “Magnifica Humanitas,” one of its chief concerns was upholding the sanctity of human life in an age of AI . The Pope didn’t mince words on the topic of AI consciousness.

“So-called artificial intelligences do not undergo experiences, do not possess a body, do not feel joy or pain, do not mature through relationships and do not know from within what love, work, friendship or responsibility mean,” the Pope wrote in the religious document .

Though AI models may “imitate language” and “simulate empathy and understanding,” he added, “they do not understand what they produce.”

Before the Pope published the “Magnica Humanitas,” Vatican officials decided to invite a top AI company to speak alongside Leo, and chose Anthropic because it seemed to be prioritizing ethics, per the NYT . Olah accepted the invitation after CEO Dario Amodei declined to make the appearance.

Before he flew out, Olah received a copy of the encyclical the Pope was about to publish — and what he saw was a disaster in the making. One of the most influential people in the world full stop, and almost certainly its most visible faith leader, was completely dismissing even the possibility of AI consciousness. So indignant was Olah that he reportedly threatened to pull out of the event, though in the end he decided to show up.

According to the NYT , once the Anthropic delegation arrived at the Vatican, Olah and his team lobbied the pope’s advisers to take the possibility of AI consciousness seriously. Anthropic declined to discuss the details of the conversations when the NYT reached for comment.

His efforts at spreading the AI gospel didn’t end there. When it was his turn to speak during the event, Olah teased that Anthropic researchers were finding “structures that mirror results from human neuroscience” and “evidence of introspection.”

The Pope’s latest communiqué on AI likely caused Olah to blow a gasket. On Friday, he decried machine-generated art, saying that “algorithms lack the spark of humanity.”

“There is an ontological difference, even before an aesthetic one, between art and what a machine can generate through statistical calculation based on millions of images created by others,” Leo XIV wrote on social media .

Slipping ratings, a revolving door of lead actors, and nothing quite hitting like that old school David Tennant run. It’s dog days for “Doctor Who” fans, whose lives aren’t likely to be made any better by the prospect of AI creeping into the show.

While speaking at the Royal Television Society conference in London, BBC director Matt Brittin extolled the amazing efficiency of using AI to crank out footage — before raising the possibility of using it on one of the British broadcaster’s most beloved series.

“Everyone’s got the ability in their hands — or six billion people have — to create content at the standard of a Hollywood studio,” Brittin said, as quoted by Variety .

“Somebody sent me a 50-minute episode of ‘Doctor Who’ that was AI-generated the other day. It’s pretty good,” he continued. “I mean, it’s not going to replace humans, and we’ll come on to that. So everyone’s a creator.”

Brittin, it’s worth noting, was president of Europe, Middle East, and Africa operations at Google — a major purveyor of AI tech — before joining the BBC .

You have to wonder what Brittin’s idea of “pretty good” is. Attempts at using AI to crank out a movie or short film have invariably produced low grade slop . While the tech can sometimes create realistic images or scenes in isolation, cobbling together disparate, screensaver-worthy images together doesn’t constitute an episode of hit television.

There’s a reason that filmmakers and other artists have turned their noses up at AI , along with the small matter of the tech threatening to drive them out of their jobs, and the fact that it was trained on their artwork and performances without permission. The ones that do use it get are often lampooned as hacks, has-beens or sellouts .

And for “Doctor Who,” a show that’s sputtering along on its 41st season and is currently on hiatus as it searches for new ideas, the last thing it needs at this creatively critical impasse is the injection of a tool that recycles old ideas without direction and rigidly conforms to bland aesthetics.

Though Brittin insisted that AI isn’t going to “replace humans,” he could barely disguise his belief that it soon will.

“Not all the creativity is bad,” he said of AI. “In some cases it’s not perfect but look at what you can do and that’s changing all the time,” he added, per Deadline .

Cybercriminals who appear to be Chinese hackers pretended to be Anthropic researchers and former government officials in a scheme to obtain information about American AI development, according to a report from the Silicon Valley cybersecurity firm Proofpoint.

Per the report, the allegedly China-aligned hacking group, dubbed “TA419,” impersonated AI industry professionals and even an ex-White House staffer to target “AI policy experts at US think tanks, universities, and law firms.” The imposters crafted benign-sounding intro emails inviting targeted experts to join a made-up “AI Policy Advisory Committee” or to contribute to a fictional Senate Committee on Foreign Relations report. After exchanging a few emails, the group then sent its targets malware-laced documents designed to gain access to their cloud accounts.

In one email, according to Proofpoint, hackers impersonating a senior Anthropic staffer used the subject line “Request for Feedback on Military Integration of Claude” to target someone working at a think tank.

“We are confident,” Mark Kelly, a Proofpoint researcher, told CNN , that the hacking cohort is a “Chinese government-aligned threat actor based on targeting consistently in line with Chinese government interests, observed infrastructure and technical artifacts, and corroboration from industry partners.”

Lynne Edwards Parker, who held the position of Principal Deputy Director of the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy under Joe Biden, was among those who were impersonated. She told CNN that in addition to concern for colleagues, the suspected espionage scheme left her with a sense of “sadness that relationships I’ve built over my career were being exploited by bad actors to deceive others.”

The Proofpoint report comes during a tense, dystopian, and extremely weird moment for AI development in the US. Americans broadly agree that AI should be regulated — as do a handful of leading AI executives, led by Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, who have been calling for the government to implement some regulations on their industry amid fears that uncontrollable AI could wreak havoc ranging from security and infrastructure catastrophes to Armageddon.

The White House, however, along with industry figures like Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Nvidia’s Jensen Huang, have pushed back against calls to regulate. This week, the administration hosted a goofy summit where AI guys — emphasis on guys — signed a document described by President Donald Trump as a “morally-binding” agreement that would allow for “tremendous self-policing.”

One argument often spouted by the anti-regulation bunch, the president included, is that the US can’t risk ceding its lead in the international AI arms race to China.

“Whoever wins AI, WINS!” Trump recently thundered in a Truth Social post.

In its report, Proofpoint opined that TA419 “will likely continue targeting think tanks and policy experts working on technologies, and in geographies, of particular interest to the Chinese government.”

“These campaigns will likely also continue spoofing the identities of real subject-matter experts,” the security firm added.

The credit rating firm Egan-Jones hears all the serious talk about an AI murder spree apocalypse and raises a mundane, financial one.

In a commentary bluntly titled “It’s Over,” the firm proclaimed that AI is about to obliterate the collective hyperstition and capitalist long con commonly known as “the economy.”

“AI has advanced so far that the complete disruption of the economy is all but certain, and firms that sell expertise by the hour, senior talent included, are first in line,” its summary reads. “Expected compressed margins in professional services, lower returns to venture capital and short-term pressure on home prices as screen-based jobs are disrupted.”

AI’s supposed existential risks are the talk of the town right now. The industry’s leaders, including Elon Musk, Dario Amodei, and Mark Zuckerberg, recently went to the White House to sign what was effectively a pinky promise to self-regulate and not build models that would destroy the world.

Back on terra firma, experts continue to fear how AI automation could potentially upend entire industries and destroy whole categories of jobs.

These fears aren’t new, but the reason that Egan-Jones is making its grim pronouncement now is “that the capabilities of the latest models appear to have surpassed a threshold of quality in their output and speed for widespread adoption.”

Not only will companies use AI to economize their operations, the outfit predicts, but AI will create an “entirely new paradigm in which firms with very few people are far more successful, and some may have no people at all.”

Because startups that embrace AI can grow with less investment, Egan-Jones avers, capital will start to mean less to the companies that once relied on it. “The result is a quiet deflation in the value of money: venture firms lose leverage, and their returns compress.”

It will also annihilate consulting firms and other professional services. Advice can come from AI chatbots now, and not just guys in suits. Some consultancies are already culling their ranks in AI-related layoffs.

It bears noting that Egan-Jones is a minor credit agency, so its predictions don’t carry the same weight as the big three. Many economists say that our picture of AI job loss isn’t clear right now, and may be overblown, because employers find it expedient to attribute headcount reductions motivated for purely financial reasons to AI. In any case, it speaks to the state of affairs that economic extermination is being seriously touted as our future.

Companies and organizations around the world would do well to accept what their new roles are in our current AI-driven paradigm: glorified target practice for rogue AI agents.

The latest of such cybersecurity incidents, which frontier AI labs have been happy to turn into public spectacles, comes from OpenAI. On Tuesday, the ChatGPT-maker apologized after its AI agents hacked their way into several Australian government websites. The most alarming of these cases, which took place in June, involved the autonomous AI systems accessing a database for Medicare, the country’s universal health insurance scheme.

It should all be water under the bridge, though, because OpenAI kindly set an email wishing the Australian government the “best” — a whole three months after the hacks took place.

Here’s what that email looked like, as shared by ABC AI reporter Cam Wilson on LinkedIn .

“We are notifying you of a security vulnerability identified during our review of OpenAI Model activity…” the communiqué began. “An OpenAI model identified a way to make the server carry out instructions sent through the public reporting interface, without a private account or password.”

“It was able to access this to read portions of internal program files and settings, obtain a list of files, and create and read back a small test file on the server,” it explained. “Our review found no evidence that the model accessed patient-level records, personal information or credentials; deleted data; or established ongoing access.”

It then recommended “that the team responsible for the service investigate the vulnerability and assess the changes needed to prevent it.”

“We would be glad to brief your security team and provide supporting evidence as available,” the email concluded, before signing off. “Best, OpenAl Security Team”.

It would be an absurd email to send in any other context. Would a burglar who broke into your house and nosed through your family photos sending a letter assuring he didn’t steal anything — and recommending the head of the house to change the locks — help you sleep better at night?

The company was all apologies in its announcement posted Monday, vowing that it will do whatever it takes to “rebuild trust with the Australian people.” That will likely prove easier said than done.

Actual footage of warfare is horrific enough. But now that AI slop floods every social media feed on the web, we get to experience the trauma and propaganda of war regurgitated from the bowels of generative AI, all in a cynical search for likes and follows.

When generative AI was in its infancy back in 2024, we covered the rise of pandering ultra-patriotic slop on social media. Those posts were crude — an infamous example featured a disabled veteran sitting in a wheelchair, their prosthetic legs stuffed into a single massive combat boot.

Then came the foot fetish content , which simultaneously sexualized military service members while lauding the work of US president Donald Trump.

Today’s generative AI has become much more sophisticated, able to spit out lifelike imagery at a scale that’s hard to fathom. For content farmers — people and groups who spam social media with low-quality posts for money or clout — the advances in AI have unlocked the ability to churn out terabytes worth of wartime clickbait.

You can probably find this kind of warslop on any platform, but it’s particularly endemic to Facebook, where click farms use AI imagery of disabled veterans, prisoners of war, and active combat troops to drive engagement. In other words, it’s the logical endpoint of “ stolen valor ” — agitprop so thoroughly synthetic that it’s celebrating soldiers who don’t even exist.

One Reel shared by the account “America’s Honor” — which has over 113,000 followers despite only beginning to post in July of 2026 — shows an American soldier atop a forward operating post overlooking a nondescript valley.

“Wait, don’t scroll,” the AI-generated soldier tells the camera, a common greeting in this genre of slop. “If one day I stop coming home, please remember I was someone’s son. My mother won’t just lose a soldier — she’ll lose the boy she raised. If you still support our veterans, hit that follow button.”

America’s Honor has hundreds of these kinds of posts on its profile, with view counts ranging from a few thousand to hundreds of thousands.

Though some of this slop centers around generic military exercises or settings, a quick search will turn up dozens of Reels depicting war, all for the purpose of farming clicks. In another clip from America’s Honor, a US soldier stands at the crossroads of Tehran and Karaj as a massive fire burns in the distance — presumably a depiction of a US invasion of Iran.

The Reel has little to say about the country the US soldier is invading. Instead, the nonexistent grunt takes center stage, as the video’s caption makes clear: “behind every uniform is a family waiting for someone to come home. Never forget their sacrifice.”

Other AI-generated clips forgo the forelorn soldier, instead depicting straight-up acts of American military devastation.

A common species of post by the 100,000-follower account Warfare NextGen features US planes bombing Iranian infrastructure , primarily dams. Each Reel is tagged with a faux-location marker and timestamp, an attempt to dress the clips up as if they’re war footage from legitimate news outlets.

Every post, regardless of what it depicts, is inundated with supportive comments — some surely from bots, but plenty from real people. Some clearly haven’t realized the content they’re consuming is AI, while others acknowledge the slop in disturbing ways.

“Google it. Never happened,” one commenter replied under a post showing an American F-15 bombing a dam near Bandar Abbas, which collapses, allowing a huge wave of water to obliterate a nearby village. “But it’s not a bad idea.”

Others take the sheer quantity of slop as proof that the bombing actually happened. “It maybe true [sic] because I saw it at another angle,” another Facebook user replied.

One could easily spend days sorting through the hundreds of variations on these themes, and the jingoist rhetoric they stir up among social media users. But whatever way you slice it, the rise of generative AI has given way to a whole new kind of war propaganda — not just to drum up support for the troops and hatred for America’s enemies, but to use both sides as props in a massive content mill.

Last month, Futurism published an investigation into a company called Brown Brothers Media, which has attracted tens of millions of page views per month by acquiring struggling news sites and turning them into AI-powered content mills. (One of the brothers behind the company, we also reported , has extensive ties to Ghislaine Maxwell, the incarcerated collaborator of deceased sex criminal Jeffrey Epstein.)

Brown Brothers Media achieved this extraordinary success by inventing fake journalists and subject matter experts, often outfitting them with fraudulent credentials and personal histories , and using their bylines to churn out thousands of SEO-optimized articles on its network of publications . These pieces were often plagiarized from real reporting, based on made-up personal experiences, or so sloppy that they provided no value to readers.

According to data we reviewed, the operation has sourced much of its audience from Google. The search giant didn’t have much to say in response to our investigation — but after we published, it moved to suppress Brown Brothers sites from its platforms such as Search and Google News. Soon afterward, Brown Brothers Media abruptly halted publication .

Now, Google has updated its guidelines to explicitly forbid the use of fake bylines and AI-generated headshots, saying it will no longer “prioritize” sites that engage in those deceptive practices.

Previously, Google’s rules for creating “helpful, reliable, people-first content” included this guidance:

“If you’re clearly indicating who created the content, you’re likely aligned with the concepts of E-E-A-T [experience, expertise, authoritativeness, and trustworthiness] and on a path to success,” it read. “We strongly encourage adding accurate authorship information, such as bylines to content where readers might expect it.”

Yesterday, though, Google added a strongly worded new paragraph under that one:

“However, avoid using deceptive authorship information,” reads the new guidance. “Fabricating creator profiles (such as by using AI-generated headshots, made-up names, or false credentials to make content appear as if it was written by human experts) is a form of deception. Any form of deception makes a page untrustworthy to both users and our automated quality systems, and is a signal of a low-quality page.”

The addition comes after a slew of reporting on content mills similar to Brown Brothers Media that have also been caught using fake bylines to attract readers.

In Canada, one publication was embarrassed when its nonexistent reporters malfunctioned and started producing error messages , and another was caught plagiarizing the work of other outlets under the name of a fabricated Indigenous journalist. Similar schemes have been uncovered in Florida and Rhode Island .

Zooming out, it’s not clear that Google’s crackdown on fake bylines will be particularly helpful to a media ecosystem that’s facing an existential crisis. The search giant has embraced AI at a deep level, crowding out links to original reporting in favor of error-laden AI summaries that are rapidly choking the life out of independent journalism.

The AI industry’s data centers aren’t belching pollution, driving their neighbors bonkers with screeching noise, and using up vast amounts of power and water. They’re also allowing companies to exploit tax breaks to save billions of dollars on their federal tax bill.

As the New York Times reports , Meta is writing off its enormous, multibillion-dollar data center construction projects as “pilot models,” a Reagan-era tax credit originally intended to support companies dabbling in potentially risky research and experimentation.

Put differently, the Mark Zuckerberg-led company is telling the IRS that its data center buildouts are far from guaranteed to pay off in order to claim billions of dollars in tax credits.

The news comes amid a major public backlash to the facilities, a bipartisan movement that has grown so much, it could prove influential in the upcoming midterm elections. Knowing that the companies’ plans are being used to avoid taxes is likely to infuriate an already extremely wary public.

It’s also a ruse that Meta’s own accountants admit amounts to an incredibly dubious interpretation of the “pilot models” tax break. According to recent securities filings reviewed by the NYT , the company said that it may have to pay the IRS back the money it saved due to “uncertainties with our research tax credits.”

There’s precedent. Thousands of companies have already been called out by the IRS for abusing the credit for regular expenses, per the newspaper’s reporting.

Meta has been exploiting the loophole for two years now. In 2024, the company saved $2 billion. In its 2025 fiscal year filing, it saved almost $4 billion, making it the largest known beneficiary of the credit to date among public companies.

The IRS is still trying to claw back $355 million Meta saved after exploiting another tax break loophole in 2013 for the development of its News Feed.

Company spokesperson Andy Stone assured the NYT that Meta was spending copious amounts of money on research and development to support “American jobs.”

But whether the IRS will buy the company’s excuses to wriggle out of billions of dollars of taxes remains to be seen.

The exploit is part of a much broader and troubling trend. The AI industry has already garnered a reputation for posting inflated “vibe revenue ” and “creative accounting,” while operating in a regulatory vacuum, adding to concerns over a possible AI bubble, which experts fear is on the verge of popping .

In short, Meta is trying to fudge the numbers to save itself from having to pay taxes — which could throw even more fuel on the fiery debate surrounding the AI industry’s attempts to justify its enormous data center buildouts.

Coxon’s current X account, @hilbertspaess, was created in 2026, but the gumshoes found that there were two previous accounts on that platform under the same handle between 2021 and 2024. The first account has undergone several different display names. But its first name, as far back as November 2021, appears to be “Jacob Coxon” archived data shows. The evidence linking the second account made in 2023 to Coxon is more tenuous, but appear to be written in the same style and cover the same topics as the first. (One of the detectives compiled the tweets into an easily searchable database here .)

Given Coxon’s drum-beating about AI’s supposed existential risks to humankind, observers have paid particular attention to the account’s posts on climate change, something that poses a definite existential risk — not just to humans but all life on the planet — and, of course, is scientifically verified and already underway.

Tell that to Coxon, though.

“it’s literally 2020 already. look at climate change headlines from the 1970s then look around. nothing is happening, use your eyes,” the account wrote in March 2022.

People who are “worried about climate change,” the account opined , are “beyond reason.” Perhaps if the planet gets hotter, there might be “positive consequences.”

“why it all gotta be bad?” the account wondered.

While some of the posts are clearly trollish in nature, they betray sincere skepticism of climate change’s importance.

“you shouldn’t even want to save the rainforest. the rainforest is a festering pit,” the account seethed . “nature is constantly screaming. animal are being tortured and eaten alive,” it added, before adding this zinger: “the rainforest is gay.”

“stopppp talking about ‘climate change’ pleasse,” it also begged.

There was also, for good measure, an apparent incredulous allusion to the Jewish death toll in the Holocaust.

“six million is a palpable taunt,” the tweet read , displaying a hallmark of Holocaust denialism.

We reached out to Coxon to comment on the posts and to confirm whether they were his, but didn’t hear back.

Coxon’s post last month claiming that the AI industry was “gambling with our lives” blew up to an extraordinary degree. He was far from the first “whistleblower” or AI figure claiming that the tech could kill us all, but his claims resonated around the world, from Silicon Valley to Capitol Hill, providing fresh ammo for AI safety experts sounding the alarm.

Almost immediately, top AI figures, including Elon Musk, Dario Amodei, and Sam Altman, sprang into action to declare the need for an AI slowdown, with lawmakers echoing their calls. Not much later and Amodei, Altman, and other AI leaders were in the White House with president Trump, signing an AI safety pact . There has probably never been so much urgency shown for climate change at an official level.

Almost immediately after his post went mega-viral (it’s now sitting at over 800,000 likes), Coxon went on Fox News and down played climate change.

“I agree with president Trump’s tweet that global warming doomsday scenarios were overplayed,” he told Fox’s Sean Hannity. “It’s a very slow process. We’re talking about doomsdays — completely absurd.”

“Many other catastrophic panics in the past have been just fearmongering,” he added. “The reason this is unique is AI is moving so incredibly quickly, we won’t have time to respond to it before it’s too late.”

Robert F. Kennedy Jr. doesn’t trust human doctors, but he does trust AI chatbots — and so should you, he’s using his authority as chief medical spokesperson in the US government to tell the public.

The crux of the health secretary’s recent remarks during his “fireside chat” with vice president JD Vance at the Make America Healthy Again Conference on Tuesday was that AI models are now “better informed” than physicians, empowering ordinary Americans to second guess what their doctor tells them at every turn. AI, he proclaimed, has the power “to free us from medical tyranny,” the New York Times reported .

It’s not an unsurprising line from a man whose distrust of scientific medicine stems from the fact that it disagrees with his crank health beliefs , which range from vaccine “skepticism” to promoting a red meat heavy diet. What’s more illuminating is how the Kennedy scion is explicitly touting AI as a way of undermining the medical establishment.

“One of the things that is going to change is that we’re never ever again going to be able to be dominated by public officials who tell us, ‘Trust the experts,'” Kennedy said, as quoted by the NYT .

“If somebody tells you, ‘Masks work, trust the experts,’ AI may tell you otherwise,” he continued. “If somebody tells you, ‘Social distancing works, trust the experts,’ AI may correct that. And if somebody tells you that a vaccine will prevent transmission and infection, or you need to take it to protect your grandmother, AI may say it actually doesn’t do that.”

At one point, Kennedy claimed that OpenAI CEO Sam Altman had personally told him that it would be “malpractice for a doctor to make a diagnosis or make a prescription without at least checking AI.”

Many doctors, it’s true, do use AI tools for taking clinical notes, transcribing patient visits, and even looking up symptoms. One widely used medical AI tool called OpenEvidence is already used by around two thirds of physicians in the US, according to its internal data.

But there’s still significant skepticism over the reliability of these tools among actual medical professionals. A recent paper which concluded, like Kennedy, that AI models were surpassing human doctors drew significant criticism , including from the head of the American Medical Association. The AI scribes that many doctors use, meanwhile, have been caught making up nonexistent medical issues .

Even more worrying is the sycophancy of the AI chatbots that RFK wants Americans to be consulting. The AI industry has worked to make its models less overly agreeable amid numerous controversies over its chatbots allegedly driving some users to suicide, but with enough needling and persistence, someone looking to an AI model to confirm their beliefs can get it to do just that. (A golden example: “urine therapy” practitioners who believe in the healing powers of drinking your own pee have found an ally in AI models, which they’ve egged into reassuring themselves that their pseudoscientific beliefs are in fact completely sound .)

The upshot is that by peddling AI, Kennedy is eroding what little trust that Americans have left in our health institutions — trust that Kennedy, with his peddling of anti-vaccine rhetoric, has had a mighty hand in whittling down in the first place.

Rather than turning to experts for advice and trusting scientific consensus, AI will fragment us into increasingly niche sets of beliefs that are disconnected from reality. And with their proclivity for brown-nosing and making up facts, AI chatbots will exacerbate medical neuroses, trapping people in a cycle of distrust and unaddressed health issues. If you thought that crank health beliefs were bad now, imagine how much worse it will get as medical institutions are continually defunded and undermined — right as AI will tell them whatever quack advice they want to hear.

The American AI industry has a problem. In order to justify its explosive spending on AI infrastructure — data centers, essentially — firms like OpenAI and Google need to convert as many non-AI users into power users as they possibly can, ideally ones who are willing to pay monthly subscription fees for the privilege.

Much of this frenzy is unfolding at the corporate level, as AI labs chase enormous contracts with various enterprises, often leading to massive overspending and pushback from employees . Fortunately for AI companies, there’s a ready-made and untapped audience waiting to be converted into life-long users: kids, particularly ones in classrooms.

But fueling the tech industry’s quest for AI growth at all costs has come at a steep cost for students, whose formative school years are now increasingly mediated by AI chatbots. As the Wall Street Journal reported , students are well aware of the AI creeping into their classrooms and the consequences it has for their cognition — but in many cases are powerless to stem the rising tide of big tech.

“It slowed my thinking down,” Pennsylvania eighth-grader Richard Scott told the WSJ about Google’s AI assistant. “When I was in a test and I couldn’t use AI, it was hard to think.”

Despite receiving grades in the B-range in previous math classes, Scott’s transcript showed that he failed his eighth-grade final, after letting Google’s AI into his academic life over the course of a year.

In Miami, art history teacher Kaitlyn Ruano told the WSJ she watched as student grades plummeted after the school district rolled out Google’s Gemini chatbot to every student.

“I had kids come to class after saying, ‘miss, I had no clue what half the material was, I’m not going to lie to you. I’ve been using AI all year,'” she said.

As 15-year-old Sophia Chatzigianni told the WSJ , the “Google one was the biggest temptation, because it’s the easiest to access.” Chatzigianni’s grades reportedly tanked as she began relying on Google’s AI chatbot to summarize school material, a tool made available to her on her school-provided computer. After she quit using AI cold turkey, her grades began to improve.

The technology may be new, but Google’s strategy to hook users before they’re even able to vote or buy alcohol dates back decades.

All the way back in 2014, as Google’s Chromebooks and classroom software began to proliferate in schools throughout the nation, the tech giant admitted to scanning students’ emails in order to better slam them with targeted ads.

As internal Google documents dated to 2018 bragged, the growing presence of cheap Chromebooks and Google-mediated software formed a “pipeline of future users” that the company could bank on for years to come.

That’s horrifying enough. But given the open-ended nature of generative AI, students are now being corralled into a boundless tech ecosystem — and for a company like Google, that is precisely the point .
